theme: Job’s final defense, his past, his suffering, his oath
readingInstruction: Read Job 29:1-31:40. This is Job’s final speech to his friends. It has three parts: a look back at his happier past, a description of his present humiliation, and an oath of innocence. It is long, so read it in three sittings if you need to.
settingTheScene: Job’s last speech is like a legal brief. He lays out what his life was before, what it is now, and why he believes he is not at fault. It reads like an honest man’s last defense in court. He does not insult his friends in this section, and he does not curse God. He sets out his case, and then he asks God to answer. The chapters are long, but they give you the most complete portrait of Job as a person in the whole book.
observation: Job longs for “the months of old, as in the days when God watched over me” (29:2).
He remembers his authority in the city gate. The young men stepped back, and the old men rose when he came (29:7-8).
He rescued “the poor who cried for help, and the fatherless who had none to help him” (29:12).
He says, “I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame. I was a father to the needy” (29:15-16).
Now he is mocked by those whose fathers he would not have put with the dogs of his flock (30:1).
“I cry to you for help and you do not answer me; I stand, and you only look at me” (30:20).
“You have turned cruel to me; with the might of your hand you persecute me” (30:21).
“I made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin?” (31:1).
He swears that he has not been unjust to his servants, has not withheld food from the poor, has not trusted in gold, and has not rejoiced at an enemy’s ruin (31:13-30).
“Oh, that I had one to hear me! (Here is my signature! Let the Almighty answer me!)” (31:35). “The words of Job are ended” (31:40).
interpretation:
There is something moving in chapter 29. The picture of Job as the one who defended the weak is a picture of a man who really loved justice. He did not simply enjoy a position. He used it to rescue the poor. He describes himself as clothed in righteousness and justice like a robe. Nothing here is false. The narrator told you that Job was blameless, and this is what blamelessness looked like in practice.

But look at what he misses most. It is not wealth or status. It is the sense that God was watching over him. “When the Almighty was yet with me” (29:5). The loss of God’s felt presence hurts more than the loss of his children or his health. That is the right order of grief.

Chapter 30 is the opposite picture. Those who once respected him now spit at him. He says that God has become cruel to him. That is a severe statement and the narrator does not correct it here. In fact, Job is describing how things feel. He may not be right about God’s intentions, but he is honest about his experience. The Bible lets him say it.

Chapter 31 is the longest oath in the book. It is a series of “if I have” statements: if I have lusted, if I have been dishonest, if I have been unjust to my servants, if I have ignored the poor, if I have put my trust in money. Each one calls down a curse on himself if it is true. This is how people in the ancient world swore to their innocence. And look at what is covered. Job’s integrity touches his eyes, his business, his household, his generosity, and his heart. This is a man who believes that God’s law applies to every part of life.

At the end Job signs his name. “Here is my signature!” He asks God to answer. And he says, “The words of Job are ended.” He has said everything he has to say. Now he is going to wait for God.
connection: Job’s description of rescuing the poor and clothing himself in righteousness is a picture of the righteous king in Psalm 72:12-14 and Isaiah 11:4-5, and ultimately of Jesus. The “covenant with my eyes” is echoed in Jesus’ teaching in Matthew 5:27-30. James 1:27 says that pure religion is “to visit orphans and widows in their affliction.”
application:
Look at the list of Job’s oath in chapter 31. Choose one area where you want to be more faithful, such as your eyes, your honesty in business, how you treat people who work for you, or how generous you are. Write a one-sentence commitment.

Remember that the deepest loss is losing the sense of God’s presence. If you feel that loss, bring it to him honestly.

Ask yourself how you can be “eyes to the blind” to someone this week.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to search your heart and show you what is not right.
Thank Jesus for being the righteous one who truly cared for the poor.
Ask him to help you follow Christ in your relationships.
